title: López Beltrán Calls Salinas Pliego a “Vulture” and Questions Him About His Ties to Epstein, García Luna and Marcial Maciel
author: La Jornada Staff
content:
_This article by[La Jornada
Staff](https://www.jornada.com.mx/autores/de%20la%20redacci%C3%B3n) originally
appeared in the [November 9, 2026 edition of La
Jornada](https://www.jornada.com.mx/noticia/2026/11/09/politica/lopez-beltran-
llama-buitre-a-salinas-pliego-y-lo-cuestiona-por-sus-vinculos-con-epstein-
garcia-luna-y-marcial-maciel), Mexico's premier left wing daily newspaper._

**Mexico City**. Andrés Manuel López Beltrán, son of former President Andrés
Manuel López Obrador, on Monday answered one by one the questions put to him
by businessman Ricardo Salinas Pliego, whom he called "miserable" and a
"vulture," and returned to him his own list of questions about his businesses,
his taxes and his personal relationships.

In a video of about 34 minutes released on his social media, López Beltrán
maintained that the accusations by the president of Grupo Salinas are "in
reality a disguised accusation," because the businessman has no evidence to
accuse him directly, and he said the questionnaire seemed to have been written
by a child.

López Beltrán stated that he generates legitimate income, that he is up to
date on paying taxes, "unlike you," and that his economic activities are
audited by the government and the banks.

López Obrador's son also reiterated that he has never had a contract with any
level of government, neither directly nor through third parties, and that he
did not intercede for or recommend anyone to obtain one.

López Beltrán responded to Salinas Pliego's question about the murder of
Ximena Guzmán and José Muñoz, aides to Mexico City Head of Government Clara
Brugada, and told the businessman, for making political use of the crime:

> You are a miserable man, a person without values and a vulture.
>
> Andrés Manuel López Beltrán

He described both as honest and humble people, and said he hoped the material
and intellectual authors would be arrested.

## Salinas Pliego's Questionable Ties

After warning that for every question he answered he expected an answer from
the businessman, López Beltrán directed at him a list of questions about his
business career, his lawsuits and his personal relationships.

The first batch focused on Luis Cárdenas Palomino, a former associate of
Genaro García Luna. López Beltrán asked whether he was director of Adamantium,
Salinas Pliego's private security company, and whether under his management it
won contracts at airports and ports during the government of Enrique Peña
Nieto. "Isn't it logical to link you to the accusations that are also made
against Cárdenas Palomino?" he posed, mirroring the method he attributes to
the businessman. And he asked whether Salinas Pliego has a relationship with
García Luna.

López Beltrán recalled that both García Luna and Cárdenas Palomino are in
prison and accused in the United States of drug trafficking, and asked the
businessman whether he knew that the director of his company was linked to
those crimes or whether he never suspected it. He also asked whether the
contracts that Adamantium carried out at airports and ports, headed by a
person accused of drug trafficking, could have been used to facilitate
criminal activities, and how much they amounted to. "Do you think it is
morally correct to hire a former public official to win contracts in the areas
that said official coordinated from the government?" he questioned.

On another topic, López Beltrán questioned the purchase of Imevisión, the
state television network that Salinas Pliego acquired and that would later
become TV Azteca. He asked him who set the sale price and whether it is true
that the company was worth at least 10 times more than what he paid for it. He
recalled that Raúl Salinas de Gortari, brother of then-President Carlos
Salinas de Gortari, who was imprisoned for 10 years accused of crimes such as
murder, money laundering, illicit enrichment, tax fraud and embezzlement,
**lent him 30 million dollars for that operation**. He asked him whether that
loan should not have been investigated for influence peddling, illicit
enrichment and operations with resources of illicit origin and, even if legal,
whether it did not seem immoral to him to receive money from the brother of
the sitting president when the latter was selling him a state company.

He also asked him whether he ordered or authorized the armed takeover of Canal
40's transmission facilities in December 2002, and whether he considers the
use of force legitimate or legal to resolve a lawsuit or a commercial dispute.

The son of former President López Obrador also questioned whether it is true
that Salinas Pliego was a partner of Marcial Maciel, founder of the
Legionaries of Christ and accused of sexual abuse of minors. According to him,
several press accounts indicate that Maciel and the congregation owned 12% of
TV Azteca's shares.

On Jeffrey Epstein, accused of exploitation and abuse of minors, López Beltrán
stated that **the businessman 's name appears at least 77 times in the so-
called Epstein files**. He asked him to recount how many times he saw him,
what they talked about and why he agreed to see him.

## Benefits from Privatizations and Fobaproa

In the area of privatizations, he asked him about his participation in the
purchase and sale of Fertinal, another company privatized under the government
of Carlos Salinas de Gortari. He wanted to know what part of the 635 million
dollars that Pemex paid for that bankrupt company ended up in Banco Azteca and
in Arrendadora Internacional Azteca, and what is or was his relationship with
Emilio Lozoya Austin, who faces a judicial process over the purchase of
another part of the company privatized in that six-year term.

López Beltrán also asked him what economic benefits he and his family obtained
from Fobaproa and the bailout of the company Salinas y Rocha. He questioned
whether it is true that this bailout **cost the people of Mexico 4 billion
pesos** , about 505 million dollars at the time, and that the businessman
later bought the already cleaned-up company for only 77.7 million dollars.

Regarding his lawsuits abroad, he recalled that in 2005 the SEC, the federal
agency that oversees and regulates securities markets in the United States,
accused Salinas Pliego of securities fraud for 109 million dollars. According
to López Beltrán, the businessman later reached a settlement in which he paid
only 7.5 million dollars, without returning the full amount to shareholders.
He asked him whether that means he accepted having committed securities fraud
and having profited from it.

## The Lawsuits and Debts Salinas Pliego Carries

He also asked him about the lawsuit against him in the Federal Court for the
Southern District of New York, where those who bought TV Azteca debt bonds are
claiming a debt of more than 600 million dollars from him. According to him,
the plaintiffs accuse him of moving the television network's most important
assets to a new company, which he referred to as TVA 3, so that the
bondholders could not recover their money in the event of a seizure. He asked
him to confirm whether that company exists and whether it holds among its
assets the television network's broadcasting concession.

López Beltrán also asked him whether it is true that the businessman requested
a 240-million-dollar loan from Alter Bank, a tiny banking institution on the
island of Saint Lucia, in the Caribbean, which according to him has only three
employees and capital of 4 million dollars. He wanted to know what he used
that loan for, how the bank was funded to lend 70 times its capital, where the
money came from and who owns the bank or with whom he negotiated the loan.

He also mentioned a trial in England in which, he said, the businessman was
accused of resorting to the espionage firm Black Cube to illegally spy on the
lawyers of the opposing party. Maintaining that this espionage has been proven
and adjudicated, he asked him whether spying is a recurring practice in his
life and professional activity, and whether he regularly hires espionage firms
to monitor his adversaries or competitors.

On tax matters, López Beltrán asked him why, if throughout all this time he
denied owing taxes, he ended up **accepting the payment of 32 billion pesos to
the Tax Administration Service (SAT)**. He asked him to say how much he has
paid so far and how much he still has left to pay.

He also questioned him about the scheme he uses to hire the employees of his
companies. He asked him why many of them are not registered with the company
where they actually work, why they do not enjoy all their labor rights and why
part of their salaries is paid to them in another way.

On Elektra, he asked him what the highest rate or total annual cost (CAT) he
charges his customers is, and whether he thinks it fair that the neediest
people in the country have to pay up to double the price of a product because
they cannot pay for it in cash.

Regarding his commercial alliance with Western Union for sending remittances
from Mexican migrants in the United States and Canada, he asked him to specify
how much commission he charges those who send and those who receive that
money, how much he receives in business commissions for those operations and
how much he earns on the currency exchange operations.

## Relationship with Cerimedo and Gómez Mont

In the section on personal relationships, he asked him to explain his
relationship, or that of his family, with Inés Gómez Mont, who he said was
recently arrested in the United States, and above all with her husband, Víctor
Manuel Álvarez Puga, whom he described as "a famous fake-invoice dealer in
this country."

He also asked him about his relationship with Javier Negre and with the
Argentine Fernando Cerimedo, whom he described as his partner and who he said
is in prison accused of ordering the murder of his ex-wife. He wanted to know
what that political, labor and commercial relationship is based on, whether at
any time the businessman financed his political operations in Mexico or
abroad, and what his relationship is with the right-wing outlet _La Derecha
Diario_.

On his wealth, López Beltrán noted that Salinas Pliego's luxuries and
ostentatious possessions are public, and asked him how much his yacht, his
planes and his helicopters are worth, how many security personnel are at his
service and that of his family, how many properties he has for personal use
and how much money he has in his personal accounts.

He also reminded him that he has publicly stated that he holds 80% of his
personal investment portfolio in bitcoin, and asked him how much money he has
in that cryptocurrency or how many bitcoins he owns.

Since the businessman revived, under a new name, the Festival of Ideas, which
was previously called the City of Ideas, he asked him what his personal, work
or commercial relationship was with Andrés Roemer, a TV Azteca collaborator.
López Beltrán recalled that Roemer is a fugitive from justice, accused of
rape, aggravated rape and sexual abuse by 61 women.

## A Milei That Never Was

On the political front, he said that Salinas Pliego's relationship with some
officials of the United States government is public, and asked him whether he
has requested the support, help or intervention of any US official, public
servant or politician in his problems with the Mexican government.

He also reproached him for insulting the governments that emerged from the
left, which he has accused of being "narco-governments," their officials, whom
he calls "gobernícolas," and their militants, whom he calls "zurdos"
(lefties). He asked him why, then, he continues to maintain contracts and
commercial and labor relations with those same governments. "Doesn't it seem
incongruous on your part to attack, but at the same time collect from and work
with those governments?" he questioned.

He closed with a personal question: why he chose to bequeath to his family
"dishonor and public disrepute in exchange for money."

López Beltrán closed the video by reading a passage from _Pueblo_ , his
father's book, in which López Obrador talks about Salinas Pliego. In that
passage, the former president maintains that the businessman "became
enthralled with the internet" and with "the self-deception of the bots," and
that he believed those tools, together with his television networks, would
make him an opposition leader and "the great national figure, a kind of
Milei." "Only he was wrong, because Mexico is a country with a people and a
history like no other," López Beltrán reads.

## Clarifies Amílcar Matters and Contract Accusations

Regarding Jorge Amílcar Olán, he said that for more than four years he has not
seen him or had any communication with him, so he is unaware of his transfers
to Switzerland.

On the withdrawal of his US visa, he stated that the State Department gives no
justification and only gives notice by email. He reiterated that it was a
"politicking and propagandistic, Hitler-style" decision and denied any link to
organized crime. He accused Salinas Pliego of being friends with Ambassador
Ronald Johnson and with Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau, whom he
called "the visa remover."
